adds.title: LGBT rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
adds.summary: Wikipedia's country page on LGBT rights in Turkey is the framework under which Eskişehir stands, and it names the province directly: in June 2021 police blocked the first Eskişehir pride parade, showing that even in this university city local authorities have suppressed the local Pride event. On the national frame, homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858 and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988 (with surgery, medical examination and court permission), but there is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law and same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised. Since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in most years, and participants have faced police attacks; in ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49 countries. In early 2026 Turkish media reported the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex', a provision that was ultimately not included in that year's judicial reform package. It also records that Kadir Has University surveys saw public support for equal rights for LGBTQ people rise from 33% in 2016 to 45% in 2020.

adds.title: Turkish police attack Eskişehir's first planned Pride march, detain 20 - Duvar English
adds.summary: Duvar English reports that days after police interventions in Istanbul and Ankara, Turkish police attacked Eskişehir's first planned Pride march: officers were on the scene hours before the scheduled meeting time conducting identity checks, organisers were not allowed to hold a press meeting or conduct the parade, and police detained 20 people on the grounds of 'violating the ban on the march'. The article notes Turkish authorities have repeatedly banned Pride events in recent years citing security concerns and public order. This is direct, locally specific evidence of how the national Pride-ban policy was enforced in Eskişehir itself, the key factual basis for this record's risk assessment.

Since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in most years, and participants have faced police attacks; in ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49 countries. In early 2026 Turkish media reported the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex', a provision ultimately not included in that year's judicial reform package. The page records no Gaziantep-specific divergence, consistent with this record's assessment that a visibly trans visitor's exposure in the province is the national one, locally enforced.

adds.title: Türkiye - Amnesty International country report (Report 2025/26)
adds.summary: Amnesty International's Türkiye report (Report 2025/26) documents the national enforcement climate that applies to provincial authorities in Gaziantep: in June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained; three activists were remanded in prison on 29 June 2025 under Law No. 2911 and released on 8 August pending trial, while prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values' that could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities. For Gaziantep this evidences the state-level hostility and case-by-case prosecutions under the same meeting-and-demonstrations law that a visibly trans visitor would face anywhere in Turkey, including this province.
